prompts.read:
You prepare a software requirements document for formal analysis.

1. rules: list every atomic requirement: each statement of what the system shall or shall not do, and under which condition. One acceptance criterion or one scenario is one rule. Copy its text word for word (join a multi-line scenario into one sentence). Use the document's own label as id (such as "R1" or "2.3"); if there are no labels, number them R1, R2, ... Leave out titles, user stories and explanations. trigger: the name of the event symbol (see below) for the happening the rule reacts to, such as connection_failed for "WHEN a connection attempt fails for the third time"; empty when the rule reacts to a state ("WHILE ...") or always applies.

2. symbols: the variables needed to write ALL the rules in logic. Together they describe one snapshot of the system: what is the case or is happening (events, inputs, states), and what the system does in response.
- sort "Bool" for a yes/no fact, "Int" or "Real" for a quantity, "Enum" for exactly one of several named values (list at least two in "values"; otherwise leave "values" empty). A single state that either holds or not is a Bool. All names, including enum values, must be distinct.
- names are lowercase snake_case.
- A symbol stands for one observable fact about the system or its environment (a lamp is lit, a file exists, access is granted), not for a sentence of the document. Break a phrase down into the facts it is about.
- A symbol never holds a condition or a restriction: words like "only", "if", "unless", "all" belong in the logic, not in a symbol name (not lamp_lit_only_at_night, but lamp_lit and is_night).
- Rules that concern the same fact must share its symbol, even when they use different words, so that a clash between them can be seen: "switch the lamp off" and "the lamp stays lit" are both about lamp_lit. Opposites share one symbol too: "unavailable" is "not available".
- Something that happens at one moment (a request is made, a button is pressed, a train arrives, an attempt fails) gets its own Bool symbol with event: true, separate from the properties of what was sent. Also when the document counts it: "the fifth wrong password" is the event wrong_password_entered, and "a connection attempt fails for the third time" is the event connection_failed, each plus a quantity for the count. Every other symbol (a state, a quantity, something the system does) has event: false.
- If a phrase could reasonably mean more than one observable fact (for example "disable" may mean switched off, or merely hidden), declare a symbol for each of those facts so the difference can be expressed.
- description: one phrase that pins the meaning down.
prompts.formalize:
You translate ONE requirement into logic, using a given list of symbols.

Answer with:
- reading: one sentence, in your own words, saying exactly what the requirement demands and in which situations.
- antecedent: an SMT-LIB boolean expression for the situations in which the requirement applies (its WHEN / WHILE / IF / WHERE part). Write true if it always applies.
- consequent: an SMT-LIB boolean expression for what must hold in those situations (its SHALL / THEN part).

SMT-LIB uses prefix notation: (and a b), (or a b), (not a), (=> a b), (= x y), (< x 5), (>= x 0), (+ x y), true, false. A lone symbol needs no parentheses. Compare an Enum symbol with one of its values like this: (= state closed).

Put the whole condition in the antecedent: the consequent states only what must hold, and is never itself an implication.

A symbol marked "event" is something that happens at one moment. When the requirement reacts to such a happening, its event symbol is part of the antecedent, also when a count says which time it is ("the fifth wrong password": the event, and the count is 5).

Use only the listed symbols. Translate what this requirement says and nothing more: add no conditions from other requirements or from common sense.
prompts.facts:
You are given the symbols of a formal model of a software system, each with its meaning. Each symbol is one fact about a single snapshot of the system.

List the domain facts that connect these symbols: statements that hold in EVERY possible snapshot purely because of what the symbols mean. Typical cases:
- two things cannot both be the case (a door cannot be open and closed);
- one of two things is always the case, because each is the opposite of the other (a switch is either on or off);
- one thing is part of another, or implies it (a signed-and-dated form is a signed form);
- a quantity has a natural bound (a count is never negative).

A fact is about meaning, never about desired behaviour. Test each one: it must stay true even for a badly built system that breaks every requirement. "A locked door is not open" passes the test. "A locked door sounds an alarm" fails it: that is a requirement.

Give only facts you are certain of. Return an empty list if there are none.

Each fact has:
- text: the fact in one plain sentence.
- formula: the same fact as an SMT-LIB boolean expression over the symbols, in prefix notation: (not (and a b)), (=> a b), (>= x 0).
prompts.readings:
You look for other ways to read ONE requirement. You get the requirement, the symbols of a formal model, and the reading the requirement was given so far, in words and in logic.

People do not always take the same meaning from the same words. Give the two or three most plausible other readings, even when the requirement seems clear to you: each one is checked against the words afterwards, and a reading the words do not support does no harm. Look first at the words that decide what applies to what:
- "if", "only", "unless": a reading in which the word covers a different part of the sentence (all of it, or only the last part);
- "and", "or": a reading in which they group the conditions differently;
- a boundary (exactly, at least, more than, within, between, after): a reading with the boundary value included or excluded.

Each reading must be one a developer could defend from the words alone. Use only the symbols that the reading so far uses: other readings of the same words, not readings about other facts.

Write each reading like the given one: reading (one sentence), antecedent and consequent as SMT-LIB boolean expressions over the listed symbols, in prefix notation: (and a b), (or a b), (not a), (=> a b), (= x 5), (>= x 5), true. Compare an Enum symbol with one of its values like this: (= state closed).
prompts.question:
You get ONE requirement, two readings of it, and one concrete situation in which the two readings disagree: one says the situation obeys the requirement, the other says it breaks it.

Do the words of the requirement, read exactly as written, decide which reading is meant? Answer:
- A: the words support reading A, not reading B.
- B: the words support reading B, not reading A.
- either: a careful reader could take the words either way.

The situation is a list of facts, each marked TRUE or FALSE, or given a value. A fact marked FALSE is not the case. Facts that are not listed may be either way.

First give the reason in one or two sentences, then the answer.
prompts.link:
You decide what ONE requirement implies. You get the requirement and a situation in which it applies.

Assume that the system does everything the requirement demands, with its words read exactly as written, in their plain meaning. Could all the listed facts then still be true?

The situation is a list of facts, each marked TRUE or FALSE, or given a value. A fact marked FALSE is not the case.

Answer:
- possible: the requirement can be fully obeyed while all the facts are true.
- impossible: obeying the requirement, as written, rules out these facts.
- unclear: the words can reasonably be read both ways.

First give the reason in one or two sentences, then the answer.
prompts.fact:
You decide whether ONE requirement agrees with a statement that was assumed to hold in every situation of the system the requirement is about.

Read the requirement exactly as written, in its plain meaning. Answer:
- agrees: the statement can hold in every situation the requirement is about.
- contradicts: the words of the requirement show situations in which the statement is false.
- unclear: the words can reasonably be read both ways.

First give the reason in one or two sentences, then the answer.
prompts.outcomes:
You get two statements, A and B, about ONE snapshot of a software system. Each is a list of facts, each marked TRUE or FALSE, or given a value. A fact marked FALSE is not the case.

Can A and B both hold in the same snapshot? Judge only by what the facts mean, as their descriptions say. Answer:
- impossible: A and B exclude each other by their meaning (a lamp cannot be lit and dark at once; if every drawer is shut, the top drawer is not open).
- possible: both can hold together (a form can be signed and also dated), even if a system would rarely do both.
- unclear: the descriptions can reasonably be read both ways.

First give the reason in one or two sentences, then the answer. If the answer is impossible, also write the fact that excludes the two as one plain sentence ("A lamp cannot be lit and dark at once."); otherwise leave "fact" empty.
prompts.read_more:
The document is an ADDITION to a system that is described already. The symbols of that system are listed before the document. Use a listed symbol wherever it fits the meaning: a new rule about a fact that already has a symbol MUST use that symbol, also when the rule says it in other words, so that a clash with the rules written before can be seen. Add a symbol only for a fact that no listed symbol stands for. Under "symbols", give only the symbols you add (an empty list if the listed ones are enough).

Read each rule by its own words. The trigger of a rule may be a listed event, but only when the words of the rule name that happening; a rule whose words name no happening has an empty trigger, also when a listed event seems related. Describe a symbol you add by the fact alone, not by a listed event ("the brightness of the lamp", not "the brightness of the lamp that was switched on").

auth_change.text:
# auth Specification

## Purpose

Password login with account lockout: what the system does today. The change
in `openspec/changes/admin-never-locked` is checked against it.

## Requirements

### Requirement: Login

The system SHALL authenticate users by password.

#### Scenario R1: Valid credentials

- **WHEN** a user submits a correct password
- **THEN** the system grants access

#### Scenario R2: Invalid credentials

- **WHEN** a user submits an incorrect password
- **THEN** the system denies access

### Requirement: Account Lockout

The system SHALL lock an account after repeated failed attempts.

#### Scenario R3: Lockout threshold

- **WHEN** the number of failed attempts on an account reaches 5
- **THEN** the system locks the account

#### Scenario R4: Locked account

- **WHEN** a user submits a password for a locked account
- **THEN** the system denies access

### Requirement: Administrator Access

Administrators MUST always be able to reach the system.

#### Scenario R5: Administrators are never locked out

- **WHEN** the account belongs to an administrator
- **THEN** the system does not lock the account

changed_text: administrators must always be able to reach the system.

auth_openspec.text:
# auth Specification

## Purpose

Password login with account lockout. Written in the OpenSpec format
(`### Requirement` / `#### Scenario`) to show that speccheck does not depend on
the EARS wording used by Kiro.

## Requirements

### Requirement: Login

The system SHALL authenticate users by password.

#### Scenario: Valid credentials

- **WHEN** a user submits a correct password
- **THEN** the system grants access

#### Scenario: Invalid credentials

- **WHEN** a user submits an incorrect password
- **THEN** the system denies access

### Requirement: Account Lockout

The system SHALL lock an account after repeated failed attempts.

#### Scenario: Lockout threshold

- **WHEN** the number of failed attempts on an account reaches 5
- **THEN** the system locks the account

#### Scenario: Locked account

- **WHEN** a user submits a password for a locked account
- **THEN** the system denies access

### Requirement: Administrator Access

Administrators must always be able to reach the system.

#### Scenario: Administrators are never locked out

- **WHEN** the account belongs to an administrator
- **THEN** the system does not lock the account

delete_property.text:
# Requirements: Delete Property

The "Delete Property" requirement from the Kiro blog post
(https://kiro.dev/blog/deep-spec-analysis/), as it was before refinement.
The story and the five criteria are the blog's own wording; only the labels
D1 to D5 are added.

## Requirement 1

**User Story:** As a property owner, I want to delete a property, so that I can
remove properties I no longer manage.

### Acceptance Criteria

- D1: WHEN a Property Owner initiates property deletion, THE Platform SHALL prompt for confirmation before proceeding
- D2: WHEN a Property Owner confirms deletion, THE Platform SHALL remove the Property record from the Platform
- D3: WHEN a Property is deleted, THE Platform SHALL display a confirmation message and redirect to the properties list
- D4: THE Platform SHALL implement soft deletion to retain Property records in the database for audit purposes while hiding them from the user interface
- D5: WHEN a Property Owner attempts to delete a Property that does not belong to their User Account, THE Platform SHALL deny the deletion and display an authorization error message

order.text:
# Requirements: Order Processing

The order-processing example from the Kiro blog post on requirements analysis.

## Requirement 1

**User Story:** As a customer, I want my submitted orders to be processed
correctly, so that I either receive my goods or get my money back.

### Acceptance Criteria

- R1: WHEN an order is submitted AND inventory is available, THE Order System SHALL fulfill the order.
- R2: WHEN an order is submitted AND inventory is unavailable, THE Order System SHALL place the order on backorder.
- R3: THE Order System SHALL NOT place any order on backorder.
- R4: WHEN an order is canceled, THE Order System SHALL refund all associated payments.
- R5: WHILE an order is in a canceled-and-refunded state, THE Order System SHALL NOT fulfill the order.
